newsitem.title: USA: World Bank official sees broad use of U.S. policies.
newsitem.headline: World Bank official sees broad use of U.S. policies.

text.p: The policies that led to the current vibrant U.S. economy can be successfully exported globally, the chief economist of the World Bank said on Tuesday as he began his first day in that post.

Joseph Stiglitz, who a day earlier had shepherded President (Bill) Clinton's Economic Report to Congress on his last day as chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers, said the U.S. administration favoured a system in which a market-based, free-enterprise core was complemented by the role of government.

"I think those sets of ideas that have worked so effectively in the United States are the kinds of ideas that are getting increasing receptivity around the world and the challenge is to try to implement those kinds of ideas," he told a briefing for reporters.

Stiglitz said the Clinton administration had tried to take a middle path between the New Deal philosophy of President Franklin Roosevelt, in which the Federal government had a large responsibility for people's lives, and the "Reaganomics" of former President Ronald Reagan, with its reliance on individualism and only a small government role.
"We talk about government as a complement to markets, as opposed to goverments replacing markets," he said.

Stiglitz defended the administration from charges by his new boss, World Bank President James Wolfensohn, that the United States has backed away from its responsibilities to international financial institutions.
"Certainly it is not the position of this administration to disengage," he said. "The (U.S.) president has repeatedly emphsized the importance engagement is for America."
But he also said that the World Bank, because of its vast experience, has a special role to help countries use the knowledge it has accumulated to take the action to produce increased growth.
He noted that the gap between the richest and poorest countries has widened in recent years and said it was critical that this problem be addressed.
"The problems of the gap between developed countries, where income standards are rising, and the less developed countries is the most important challenge facing the world today," he told reporters.
"The bottom line is that capital markets, private markets, have shown that they can provide money if the right policies are in place," he said.
